CausalChain: HCC cells reprogram methionine metabolism -> Increased methionine adenosyltransferase activity elevates SAM and MTA levels -> SAM/MTA mediate epigenetic remodeling of tumor-infiltrating T cells -> Upregulation of exhaustion markers (e.g., PD-1, TIM-3) on T cells -> Impaired T cell cytotoxicity and enhanced immunosuppression -> Tumor progression and resistance to therapy; therefore, inhibiting methionine adenosyltransferase may reverse T cell exhaustion and restore anti-tumor immunity.
Hypothesis: In hepatocellular carcinoma, inhibition of methionine adenosyltransferase to reduce SAM and MTA production will alleviate T cell exhaustion in the tumor microenvironment, thereby restoring T cell cytotoxicity and enhancing the efficacy of checkpoint inhibitor-based immunotherapies.
Abstract: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is characterized by a complex tumor microenvironment in which metabolic reprogramming of cancer cells leads to immunosuppression and therapeutic resistance. Emerging evidence suggests that deregulated methionine metabolism results in elevated levels of S‐adenosylmethionine (SAM) and methylthioadenosine (MTA), metabolites that can drive epigenetic changes in tumor‐infiltrating lymphocytes. These alterations promote the upregulation of exhaustion markers such as PD‐1 and TIM‐3, thereby impairing cytotoxic T cell function and facilitating tumor progression. Here, we propose that inhibition of methionine adenosyltransferase, the enzyme responsible for SAM/MTA production, may alleviate T cell exhaustion in the HCC microenvironment and improve the efficacy of immunotherapies such as checkpoint inhibitors. The therapeutic targeting of these metabolic pathways could offer a novel approach to restore effective anti‐tumor immune responses in HCC.
